system.name: PSR J0437-4715
system.description: The closest millisecond pulsar to Earth at just 510 light-years away, spinning 174 times per second. It orbits a white dwarf companion — the burnt-out remnant of the very star that once fed the pulsar and spun it up to its extreme rotation rate.

j0437-pulsar.name: PSR J0437-4715
j0437-pulsar.description: A millisecond pulsar spinning 174 times per second and the nearest of its class to Earth. Its precise, clock-like pulses make it a natural laboratory for testing general relativity and detecting gravitational waves. It belongs to a pulsar timing array used by astronomers as a galaxy-scale detector.
j0437-pulsar.funFact: PSR J0437-4715 is so close and its pulses so regular that it has been used as a natural gravitational-wave detector — tiny changes in pulse timing reveal ripples in spacetime from merging black holes across the cosmos.

j0437-wd.name: J0437 White Dwarf
j0437-wd.description: A low-mass helium white dwarf — the burned-out core of the star that once donated material to the pulsar. Over billions of years, accretion from this companion spun the neutron star up from a slow rotator to the millisecond pulsar we observe today. The white dwarf is now cold and inert, an orbital relic of a long relationship.
j0437-wd.funFact: This white dwarf is thought to be one of the coolest and oldest white dwarfs known in the Milky Way — its age rivals that of the galaxy itself.
